The Stan model

Source: vignettes/stan_model.Rmd
stan_model.Rmd

fp_occu() fits one Stan program for every model in the package: the multiple-methods design of Miller et al. (2011), its observation-confirmation variant (Chambert et al., 2015), and the standard occupancy model. This article walks through it for readers who want to know exactly what is estimated, or who want to change it. The model itself is described in vignette("crywolf", package = "crywolf"); here the focus is on how it is coded. The program is a file installed with the package:

fp_stan_file()

fp_compile() copies it to the user cache directory and compiles it the first time it is needed, so later sessions reuse the executable.

Data

fp_occu() turns the fp_data object and the formulas into the list that Stan reads, which is kept in the fitted object as m$stan_data. The data block declares it:

data {
  int<lower=1> nsite;
  int<lower=1> Kbeta;
  matrix[nsite, Kbeta] X;                    // occupancy design (with intercept)

  int<lower=0> N2;                           // rows of automated occasions
  array[N2] int<lower=1> n2;                 // occasions in each row
  array[N2] int<lower=0> y2;                 // detections in each row
  array[N2] int<lower=1, upper=nsite> site2;  // sorted by site
  array[nsite] int<lower=1> start2;          // first row of each site in y2
  array[nsite] int<lower=0> len2;            // number of rows of each site
  int<lower=1> Kalpha;
  matrix[N2, Kalpha] Z;                      // detection design (column 1 = intercept)
  int<lower=1> nrec;
  array[N2] int<lower=1, upper=nrec> rec2;
  int<lower=0, upper=1> estimate_re;         // recorder random intercept on p11

  int<lower=0> Kfp;
  matrix[nsite, Kfp] Xfp;                    // false-positive design (no intercept)
  int<lower=0, upper=1> estimate_fp;

  int<lower=0> N1;                           // verified occasions (long format)
  array[N1] int<lower=0, upper=1> y1;
  array[N1] int<lower=1, upper=nsite> site1;
  array[nsite] int<lower=0, upper=1> known_present;

  int<lower=0, upper=1> obs_confirm;         // observation-confirmation design
  int<lower=0> N3;                           // confirmed occasions
  array[N3] int<lower=0, upper=3> v3;        // confirmation state
  array[N3] int<lower=1, upper=nsite> site3;
  matrix[N3, Kalpha] Z3;                     // detection design of confirmed occasions
  array[N3] int<lower=1, upper=nrec> rec3;

  real<lower=0> prior_sd_int;                // sd of Normal priors on intercepts
  real<lower=0> prior_sd_slope;              // sd of Normal priors on slopes
  real gap_mean;                             // Normal(gap_mean, gap_sd) prior on fp_gap, truncated at 0
  real<lower=0> gap_sd;
  real<lower=0> recorder_sd;                 // half-Normal(0, recorder_sd) on sigma_u
}

The occupancy design X, the detection design Z, and the false-positive design Xfp are model matrices built from the formulas. Xfp has no intercept column, because the intercept of the false-positive rate is not a free parameter (see below). Switches turn parts of the model on and off: estimate_fp = 0 gives the standard occupancy model (fp = NULL), Kfp = 0 the constant false-positive rate, estimate_re = 1 the recorder random intercept, and obs_confirm = 1 the observation-confirmation design. The prior scales are data too, which is why fp_priors() can change them without recompiling.

Binomial rows

Automated occasions do not enter one by one. Occasions of the same site with identical detection covariates (and recorder) are collapsed into one row with n2 trials and y2 detections. Given the occupancy state, the occasions of a site are independent Bernoulli trials with the same probability, so the product of their likelihoods equals the binomial likelihood without its coefficient, which does not depend on the parameters. The posterior is therefore exactly the same, and the model is much faster when detection covariates are constant within sites. With occasion-level covariates, such as the acoustic indices of the vignette("curiango", package = "crywolf") data, each occasion is its own row. Rows are sorted by site, and start2 and len2 give the first row and the number of rows of each site.

Parameters 

parameters {
  vector[Kbeta] beta;
  vector[Kalpha] alpha;
  vector[nrec] u_raw;
  real<lower=0> sigma_u;
  real<lower=0> fp_gap;
  vector[Kfp] gamma_fp;
  real delta0;
}
transformed parameters {
  vector[nrec] u = sigma_u * u_raw;
  real gamma0 = alpha[1] - fp_gap;
}

The recorder effects are written as sigma_u * u_raw, with u_raw standard normal (the non-centred parametrization), which samples better when there are few recorders or little information about their variance.

The false-positive intercept is not a parameter of its own: gamma0 = alpha[1] - fp_gap, with fp_gap constrained to be positive. Because column 1 of Z is the intercept, alpha[1] is the logit of true detection at the reference values of the covariates (all zero), and the gap keeps the false-positive rate below it there. Without this constraint, the likelihood has a second mode in which occupied and unoccupied sites swap roles, and the sampler could visit either.

Likelihood

The occupancy state z_i is discrete, so Stan cannot sample it. The function site_loglik() sums it out for each site in a range of sites, from a to b:

functions {
  // Marginal log-likelihood of sites a to b, with the latent state z summed
  // out. The automated (and confirmed) rows of these sites are contiguous.
  vector site_loglik(int a, int b, matrix X, vector beta, matrix Z, vector alpha,
                     real gamma0, matrix Xfp, vector gamma_fp, vector u,
                     array[] int rec2, int estimate_re, int estimate_fp, int Kfp,
                     vector y2v, vector n2v, array[] int site2,
                     array[] int start2, array[] int len2, array[] int any_det2,
                     vector n1v, vector s1v, real delta0,
                     array[] int known_present, int obs_confirm,
                     array[] int v3, array[] int site3, matrix Z3,
                     array[] int rec3, array[] int start3, array[] int len3) {
    int ns = b - a + 1;
    vector[ns] lpsi = X[a:b] * beta;
    vector[ns] lp10 = rep_vector(gamma0, ns);
    if (Kfp > 0) lp10 += Xfp[a:b] * gamma_fp;
    vector[ns] occ = rep_vector(0, ns);
    vector[ns] unocc = rep_vector(0, ns);

    // automated occasions, as binomial rows; log_inv_logit(x) = x - log1p_exp(x)
    // and log1m_inv_logit(x) = -log1p_exp(x)
    int r0 = start2[a];
    int nr = start2[b] + len2[b] - r0;
    if (nr > 0) {
      int r1 = r0 + nr - 1;
      vector[nr] y = y2v[r0:r1];
      vector[nr] n = n2v[r0:r1];
      vector[nr] lp11 = Z[r0:r1] * alpha;
      if (estimate_re == 1) lp11 += u[rec2[r0:r1]];
      array[nr] int loc;
      for (k in 1:nr) loc[k] = site2[r0 + k - 1] - a + 1;
      vector[nr] l11;
      vector[nr] l10;
      if (estimate_fp == 1) {
        vector[nr] lp10_n = lp10[loc];
        l10 = y .* lp10_n - n .* log1p_exp(lp10_n);
        if (obs_confirm == 1) {
          // log(1 - p11) = log(1 - s1) + log(1 - s0)
          vector[nr] lq11 = -log1p_exp(lp11) - log1p_exp(lp10_n);
          l11 = y .* log1m_exp(lq11) + (n - y) .* lq11;
        }
      }
      if (obs_confirm == 0) l11 = y .* lp11 - n .* log1p_exp(lp11);
      for (i in 1:ns) {
        int s = a + i - 1;
        if (len2[s] > 0) {
          occ[i] = sum(segment(l11, start2[s] - r0 + 1, len2[s]));
          if (estimate_fp == 1) unocc[i] = sum(segment(l10, start2[s] - r0 + 1, len2[s]));
        }
      }
    }
    if (estimate_fp == 0) {
      for (i in 1:ns) if (any_det2[a + i - 1] == 1) unocc[i] = negative_infinity();
    }

    // verified occasions, as counts per site
    occ += s1v[a:b] * log_inv_logit(delta0) + (n1v[a:b] - s1v[a:b]) * log1m_inv_logit(delta0);

    // confirmed occasions (observation-confirmation design)
    if (obs_confirm == 1) {
      int q0 = start3[a];
      int nq = start3[b] + len3[b] - q0;
      if (nq > 0) {
        int q1 = q0 + nq - 1;
        vector[nq] lp11_3 = Z3[q0:q1] * alpha;
        if (estimate_re == 1) lp11_3 += u[rec3[q0:q1]];
        for (k in 1:nq) {
          int i = site3[q0 + k - 1] - a + 1;
          int v = v3[q0 + k - 1];
          real ls1 = log_inv_logit(lp11_3[k]);
          real lq1 = log1m_inv_logit(lp11_3[k]);
          real ls0 = log_inv_logit(lp10[i]);
          real lq0 = log1m_inv_logit(lp10[i]);
          occ[i] += (v >= 2 ? ls1 : lq1) + (v % 2 == 1 ? ls0 : lq0);
          unocc[i] += v >= 2 ? negative_infinity() : (v == 1 ? ls0 : lq0);
        }
      }
    }

    vector[ns] ll;
    for (i in 1:ns) {
      real occ_branch = log_inv_logit(lpsi[i]) + occ[i];
      ll[i] = known_present[a + i - 1] == 1
              ? occ_branch
              : log_sum_exp(occ_branch, log1m_inv_logit(lpsi[i]) + unocc[i]);
    }
    return ll;
  }

  // partial sum over a slice of sites, for reduce_sum()
  real partial_loglik(array[] int slice, int a, int b, matrix X, vector beta,
                      matrix Z, vector alpha, real gamma0, matrix Xfp,
                      vector gamma_fp, vector u, array[] int rec2,
                      int estimate_re, int estimate_fp, int Kfp,
                      vector y2v, vector n2v, array[] int site2,
                      array[] int start2, array[] int len2, array[] int any_det2,
                      vector n1v, vector s1v, real delta0,
                      array[] int known_present, int obs_confirm,
                      array[] int v3, array[] int site3, matrix Z3,
                      array[] int rec3, array[] int start3, array[] int len3) {
    return sum(site_loglik(a, b, X, beta, Z, alpha, gamma0, Xfp, gamma_fp, u,
                           rec2, estimate_re, estimate_fp, Kfp, y2v, n2v, site2,
                           start2, len2, any_det2, n1v, s1v, delta0,
                           known_present, obs_confirm, v3, site3, Z3, rec3,
                           start3, len3));
  }
}

For site i, occ[i] accumulates the log-likelihood of all its data if the site is occupied and unocc[i] if it is not; the site’s contribution is then

\log\left[\psi_i \exp(\text{occ}_i) + (1 - \psi_i) \exp(\text{unocc}_i)\right],

computed with log_sum_exp() for numerical stability. Three cases shortcut it:

  • A site with a verified detection (known_present) must be occupied, so only the first term is kept.
  • Under the standard model (estimate_fp = 0), an automated detection also proves occupancy, so unocc[i] is set to -\infty.
  • Under the observation-confirmation design, an occasion confirmed to hold a true observation (v_3 \geq 2) rules out the unoccupied state in the same way.

The per-occasion terms are computed as vectors and summed by site with segment(), which works because the rows of each site are contiguous. For the automated occasions the binomial log-likelihood is written as y \eta - n \log(1 + e^{\eta}), where \eta is the linear predictor; this equals y \log p + (n - y) \log(1 - p) with p the inverse logit of \eta, but needs one transcendental function per row instead of two. The verified occasions enter as the number of occasions and detections of each site, which gives the same sum as one Bernoulli term per occasion.

Parallel likelihood

Most of the computing time goes to the automated occasions: in the vignette("curiango", package = "crywolf") data, with 97,806 one-minute occasions and a recorder effect, they took about 90% of the time spent evaluating the log density. Because sites are independent given the parameters, the model block adds them up with reduce_sum(), which splits the sites into slices and evaluates the slices on different threads. partial_loglik() is the sum of site_loglik() over one slice; each slice reads only its own rows of the automated and confirmed occasions, located with start2 and len2 (and their counterparts for the confirmed occasions, built in transformed data).

fp_compile() builds the model with threading enabled, and fp_occu(threads_per_chain = ) sets the number of threads of each chain. With one thread the sum is computed serially, as before. With more, only the order of the additions changes, so the log density differs from the serial one by floating-point rounding (around 10^{-16} in relative terms). Chains with the same seed then follow the same path for a while and drift apart later, as they would on another computer, and the posterior is the same. The gain is largest when there are many occasions: keep parallel_chains * threads_per_chain at or below the number of physical cores.

Priors and model block 

model {
  beta[1]        ~ normal(0, prior_sd_int);
  if (Kbeta > 1)  beta[2:Kbeta]   ~ normal(0, prior_sd_slope);
  alpha[1]       ~ normal(0, prior_sd_int);
  if (Kalpha > 1) alpha[2:Kalpha] ~ normal(0, prior_sd_slope);
  u_raw          ~ std_normal();
  sigma_u        ~ normal(0, recorder_sd);
  fp_gap         ~ normal(gap_mean, gap_sd);
  gamma_fp       ~ normal(0, prior_sd_slope);
  delta0         ~ normal(0, prior_sd_int);

  target += reduce_sum(partial_loglik, site_index, 1, X, beta, Z, alpha, gamma0,
                       Xfp, gamma_fp, u, rec2, estimate_re, estimate_fp, Kfp,
                       y2v, n2v, site2, start2, len2, any_det2, n1v, s1v, delta0,
                       known_present, obs_confirm, v3, site3, Z3, rec3, start3,
                       len3);
}

All priors are on the logit scale and are listed with their defaults in ?fp_priors. The model block adds the sum over sites, computed by reduce_sum(), to the log density.

Generated quantities 

generated quantities {
  vector[nsite] log_lik;
  real p11_ref = obs_confirm == 1
                 ? 1 - (1 - inv_logit(alpha[1])) * (1 - inv_logit(gamma0))
                 : inv_logit(alpha[1]);
  real p10_ref = estimate_fp == 1 ? inv_logit(gamma0) : 0.0;
  real p10_bar = 0;
  real r11 = inv_logit(delta0);
  {
    vector[nsite] lp10 = rep_vector(gamma0, nsite);
    if (Kfp > 0) lp10 += Xfp * gamma_fp;
    if (estimate_fp == 1) p10_bar = mean(inv_logit(lp10));
    log_lik = site_loglik(1, nsite, X, beta, Z, alpha, gamma0, Xfp, gamma_fp, u,
                          rec2, estimate_re, estimate_fp, Kfp, y2v, n2v, site2,
                          start2, len2, any_det2, n1v, s1v, delta0,
                          known_present, obs_confirm, v3, site3, Z3, rec3,
                          start3, len3);
  }
}

log_lik holds one value per site, with z_i summed out, so loo() on a fitted model gives leave-one-site-out cross-validation: a site with all its occasions is the unit left out. p11_ref and p10_ref are the true- and false-detection probabilities at the reference values of the covariates, p10_bar is the false-positive rate averaged over the sites in the data, and r11 is the detection probability of the verified method (p_verified in the output of fp_occu()).

Modifying a copy

To change the model, for example its priors’ families or the structure of a submodel, edit a copy of the file and fit it with ‘cmdstanr’ directly, using the data list that fp_occu() prepared:

file.copy(fp_stan_file(), "my_fp_occu.stan")
# ... edit my_fp_occu.stan ...
sim <- simulate_fp(seed = 1)
m <- fp_occu(sim$data, occ = ~ x, fp = ~ 1, random_recorder = FALSE)  # for the data list
my_model <- cmdstanr::cmdstan_model("my_fp_occu.stan")
my_fit <- my_model$sample(data = m$stan_data, chains = 4, parallel_chains = 4,
                          adapt_delta = 0.95)
my_fit$summary(c("beta", "alpha", "fp_gap", "p10_ref"))

A copy compiled without cpp_options = list(stan_threads = TRUE) runs the likelihood on one thread per chain, which gives the same results. The result is a CmdStanMCMC object with the Stan names of the parameters (beta, alpha, gamma0, …), not an fp_occu object, so the methods of crywolf do not apply to it. If the edit adds data, add the new elements to the list before sampling. fp_ppc() recomputes the likelihood in R from the posterior draws, so it describes the original model, not an edited one.

References

Chambert, T., Miller, D. A. W., & Nichols, J. D. (2015). Modeling false positive detections in species occurrence data under different study designs. Ecology, 96, 332–339. https://doi.org/10.1890/14-1507.1

Miller, D. A., Nichols, J. D., McClintock, B. T., Grant, E. H. C., Bailey, L. L., & Weir, L. A. (2011). Improving occupancy estimation when two types of observational error occur: non-detection and species misidentification. Ecology, 92, 1422–1428. https://doi.org/10.1890/10-1396.1
